back: A software development method based on frequent cycles, best known for its technical practices.
Communication, simplicity, feedback, courage, respect.
Two developers work at one computer: one writes, the other reviews, and they swap often.
Write the test before the code, then write just enough code to pass it. Also called test-driven development.
Improving the internal structure of code without changing what it does.
Everyone's work is merged and tested frequently, so problems surface early.
Anyone on the team may improve any part of the code.
Scrum: managing the work (roles, events, artifacts). XP: engineering practices. Often used together.
A philosophy aimed at maximizing customer value while minimizing waste.

front: Seven principles of lean software development
back: Eliminate waste; amplify learning; decide as late as possible; deliver as fast as possible; empower the team; build quality in; optimize the whole.
Anything that does not add value for the customer: partially done work, extra features, waiting, handoffs, task switching, defects.
Treats each product idea as a hypothesis: build a minimum viable product, measure with real customers, learn, then persevere or pivot.
The Lean Startup loop for testing an MVP with real customer data.
Changing direction, based on evidence, before investing further time and money.
A human-centered approach to problem-solving that starts from understanding user needs through observation and empathy.
Visual sign or card.
A board of columns, one per state of work, with cards that move across. Simplest form: To Do, Doing, Done.

front: Six core properties of the Kanban Method
back: Visualize the workflow; limit WIP; manage flow; make process policies explicit; implement feedback loops; improve collaboratively.
The maximum number of items allowed in a column at one time. A full column means stop starting and help finish.
When the team finishes an item, it pulls the next one in. Work is not pushed onto people.

front: Main difference between Kanban and Scrum
back: Kanban has continuous flow with no prescribed iterations or roles. Scrum has fixed-length sprints and three defined roles.
When work arrives unpredictably, or when the team cannot change its structure yet. 'Start where you are.'
A family of methods whose rigor is chosen by team size and criticality, identified by colors (Clear, Yellow, Orange, Red).
People sitting together pick up information by overhearing. A property of Crystal.
Organized around features: small capabilities with business value. Plan, design and build by feature.
Dynamic Systems Development Method. Fixes time, cost and quality at the start and prioritizes scope to fit.
A representative from each Scrum team meets the others regularly to coordinate work and remove cross-team impediments.
Scaled Agile Framework: patterns for scaling across team, program and portfolio levels, organized around value streams.
Large Scale Scrum: several teams with one product backlog, one product owner, one definition of done and one sprint.
A tool kit that helps a team choose its way of working from agile, lean and traditional practices. 'Context counts.'
